statement: In healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein in a laboratory, with salt water given to the same people on another day as the comparison in every study read here in full but one open study, where the comparison was the same people's drug-free baseline, perception, thinking and the sense of self change during the session; where symptoms were rated again after the infusion stopped, they had gone or nearly gone within about a quarter of an hour to half an hour of its end (Krystal et al., 1994; Malhotra et al., 1996), and nothing read here rated them later. A 2020 meta-analysis of 36 within-person placebo-controlled studies in 725 healthy volunteers, whose confidence the editors rate low, found higher clinician-rated symptom scores under ketamine than under salt water on every pooled measure: total 1.50 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.77; 25 studies), psychosis-like ('positive') 1.55 (1.29 to 1.81; 21 studies) and withdrawn or blunted ('negative') 1.16 (0.96 to 1.35; 22 studies) standard deviations of the within-person difference, the psychosis-like effect being the larger of the two (difference 0.36, 0.12 to 0.61), a comparison its authors qualify because the two analyses did not rest on exactly the same studies and because they call the withdrawn or blunted effect large as well (Beck et al., 2020). In that pooled set the comparison was not always made on another day: the dummy condition was salt water in 35 of its 36 studies and not reported in one, and in its total-symptom analysis 2 of the 19 studies classed by day gave both conditions on the same day, where the pooled effect was larger (2.29, 1.69 to 2.89, against 1.39, 1.12 to 1.66 in the 17 that used separate days; P = .007), which the authors suggest could reflect unblinding or better control of day-to-day variation. The review gives no recovery time, states that the time course of these effects has still to be characterised, and took its ratings 1 to 120 minutes after the infusion began in the 17 studies that report the timing, so nothing in it was measured after the session. Those pooled figures are peak values, taken at each study's largest amount and at the rating time with the highest score, so they are the largest effects the studies saw; the studies also disagreed widely about size (I2 65% to 76%, the three values printed in the review's Results, whose abstract instead prints a range of 77% to 83% that matches none of them) and showed small-study asymmetry (Egger z 4.27 to 5.12), with trim-and-fill estimates of 1.37, 1.49 and 1.09. In the single studies read here the picture is the same. In 18 volunteers (study conditions: 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes, test days in randomized order), scores for conceptual disorganization, hallucinatory behaviour, suspiciousness and unusual thought content rose at the larger amount but not at the smaller or after salt water, as did withdrawal and blunting, dissociation (CADSS) and self-rated perceptual change; the authors state scores returned to baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end of the infusion, and describe what was rated as hallucinatory behaviour as distortions of real stimuli rather than hallucinations, while also describing ideas of reference with paranoid content and loosening of associations at the larger amount (Krystal et al., 1994). In 15 volunteers given a 1-hour infusion the 18-item BPRS total rose from 19.3 (SEM 0.4) to 27.5 (1.6) at 55 minutes and was 21.5 (1.4) at 90 minutes, against 19.1, 18.7 and 18.7 after salt water, carried by thought disorder (3.0 to 6.3) and withdrawal-retardation (3.3 to 6.6), each a three-item score whose floor is 3, while the hallucinations item did not differ (1.2 against 1.0, p = 0.190) and the hostility-suspiciousness score did not change at all (F = 0.1, p = .90); the 90-minute value, 30 minutes after the end of the infusion, is not marked as differing from the salt-water day, and nothing was rated later (Malhotra et al., 1996). In 15 men given three fixed infusions aimed at steady blood levels, psychosis-like scores and a negative-symptom scale rose with the condition (F3,42 = 21.84 and 10.55), the authors called the syndrome mild, and no abnormal symptoms were found at an abbreviated, unblinded check about 48 hours later; in that study the item scored for hallucinatory behaviour was deliberately widened so that distortions of perception counted on it, and the authors detected no formal thought disorder or language disorganisation during the conditions tested apart from modest changes on one negative-symptom subscale, so its psychosis-like rise is not evidence of hallucinations; that study is also one of the 36 pooled above, so it is not separate support for the pooled figures (Newcomer et al., 1999). In an open study without a dummy condition, symptoms began on average 4.5 minutes after the start of the infusion (Vollenweider, Leenders, Scharfetter, et al., 1997). What these studies cannot settle is how far the state resembles a psychiatric illness: ego-pathology scores were about two thirds of published values for people with first-episode schizophrenia and two of the five dimensions were clearly less affected, with no patients studied in that paper (Vollenweider, Leenders, Øye, et al., 1997), and the authors of the open study limit their model to the start of acute psychotic episodes. Blinding is the weak point of the whole literature: the visible signs (blurred vision in 8 of 18 people at the larger amount in one study, with nystagmus in about half of them and vomiting in 2) make it unlikely that raters or participants stayed unaware of the condition, and no study read reports a blinding check. All of this describes one session with ketamine in the body in screened volunteers, not repeated or non-medical use.
plain: In lab studies, healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein felt and showed changes in perception, thinking and their sense of self that people rating them scored much higher than after a dummy infusion of salt water in the same people. In one open study there was no dummy day at all: the comparison was the same people before the drug. Pooling 36 such studies in 725 volunteers, the ketamine scores were well above the salt-water scores on every measure, and most so for psychosis-like experiences. Some of them gave the salt water on the same day, not another day (2 of the 19 that one analysis could sort by day). The effects were strong during the infusion. Where people were rated again after it stopped, the scores were back to about their usual level within about a quarter of an hour to half an hour. That comes from two single studies: the 36 pooled studies measured nothing after the session. What was scored as hallucinations was mostly distortions of real sights and sounds, not seeing things that were not there. People also became suspicious and their thinking became muddled. The pooled numbers are peak values from each study's largest amount, and the studies disagree a lot about how big the effects are.
population: Healthy adults screened to exclude psychiatric illness and, in most studies, previous ketamine use: 18, 15 and 15 people in the three laboratory studies read in full, 10 in the open imaging study, and 725 volunteers (mostly men) in the 36 studies pooled by the 2020 meta-analysis
exposure: A single subanaesthetic amount of ketamine into a vein during the session (study conditions: 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes; a 0.12 mg/kg bolus then 0.65 mg/kg over 1 hour; three fixed infusions aimed at steady blood levels over 2 hours; a 20 mg induction amount then 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min for 60 minutes in the open study; in the pooled studies, each study's largest amount, almost all given as a bolus followed by an infusion)
comparator: Salt water (saline) given to the same people on another day, or, in the open study, the same people's drug-free baseline scan
outcome: Clinician-rated and self-rated psychosis-like, withdrawn or blunted, dissociative and perceptual experiences during the session, and how quickly they pass
magnitude: Beck et al. (2020), healthy volunteers, peak within-person standardized mean change (ketamine against placebo): total 1.50 (95% CI 1.23-1.77; 25 studies, 491 people; I2 75.7%, Q 96.57), positive 1.55 (1.29-1.81; 21 studies, 513 people; I2 74.9%, Q 81.40), negative 1.16 (0.96-1.35; 22 studies, 527 people; I2 64.6%, Q 66.55), all P < .001; positive minus negative 0.36 (0.12-0.61), P = .004; Egger z = 4.27, 5.06 and 5.12, all P < .001; trim-and-fill 1.37 (1.07-1.67), 1.49 (1.18-1.80) and 1.09 (0.89-1.30); in the total-symptom analysis, same-day conditions (2 studies) 2.29 (1.69-2.89) against different-day (17 studies) 1.39 (1.12-1.66), P = .007 for the difference (19 of its 25 studies classed by day); blinding status not a significant moderator of any outcome; the abstract's I2 range of 77%-83% matches none of the three values in the Results. Krystal et al. (1994), n = 18: four key positive items dose F2,34 = 72.0, dose x time F8,136 = 22.9; three key negative items F8,136 = 18.0; CADSS total (n = 17) F6,96 = 46.0; Perceptual Aberration F6,102 = 20.0, all P = .0001; significant rises at 0.5 mg/kg only, at the 10- and 80-minute ratings. Malhotra et al. (1996), n = 15: BPRS total 19.3 (SEM 0.4) to 27.5 (1.6) at 55 minutes and 21.5 (1.4) at 90 minutes against 19.1, 18.7, 18.7; thought disorder 3.0 to 6.3 (floor 3); hallucinations item 1.2 against 1.0, t = 1.38, p = 0.190 (the paper does not say whether the spread printed with its item means is a standard deviation or a standard error); hostility-suspiciousness unchanged, F = 0.1, p = .90. Newcomer et al. (1999), n = 15 men: BPRS positive F3,42 = 21.84, SANS total F3,42 = 10.55, BPRS negative F3,42 = 2.89 (p = 0.047). Vollenweider, Leenders, Scharfetter, et al. (1997), n = 10, open: APZ global 37.00 (SD 12.63), ego-pathology global 23.40 (SD 5.85); first symptoms at 4.5 minutes.

evidence.locator: Results > BPRS scores > Positive symptoms of schizophrenia, 1st paragraph, and > Negative symptoms of schizophrenia (p. 203, continuing on p. 204); Figure 1
evidence.extracted: In 18 healthy volunteers the four key positive items rose with the amount given (dose F2,34 = 72.0, time F4,68 = 19.3, dose x time F8,136 = 22.9, all P = .0001): neither salt water nor 0.1 mg/kg changed them, while at 0.5 mg/kg the rise from baseline was significant at the 10-minute (t5,136 = 9.4) and 80-minute (t5,136 = 12.8) ratings, P < .01, and stayed significant after adjusting for the salt-water day. The three key negative items behaved likewise (dose F2,34 = 34.6, time F4,68 = 28.0, dose x time F8,136 = 18.0), with a significant rise at 0.1 mg/kg only at the 80-minute rating (t5,136 = 2.56, P < .05) and at 0.5 mg/kg at both (t5,136 = 9.1 and 12.6, P < .01). The authors state that positive symptom scores returned to baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end of the infusion.

evidence.locator: Results > Perceptual alterations > Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale, 1st paragraph and the paragraph on the subscales; > Perceptual Aberration Subscale of the Wisconsin Psychosis Proneness Questionnaire, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Dissociative scores (CADSS total, n = 17) rose with the amount given (dose F2,32 = 65.0, time F3,48 = 46.8, dose x time F6,96 = 46.0, all P = .0001): salt water produced no rise at any time, the rise at 0.1 mg/kg was not significant (t4,96 = 2.56, P < .1), and at 0.5 mg/kg the rises at 10 (t4,96 = 9.4) and 80 minutes (t4,96 = 18.8) were significant, P < .01. All five subscales defined by the authors (body perception, environmental perception, feelings of unreality, memory impairment, time perception) showed significant dose x time interactions, F6,96 from 17.6 to 30.0. Self-rated perceptual change (n = 18) behaved the same way (dose F2,34 = 35.4, time F3,51 = 26.7, dose x time F6,102 = 20.0), and the peak clinician-rated and self-rated changes were not significantly correlated with each other.

evidence.locator: Results > BPRS scores > Positive symptoms of schizophrenia, 2nd paragraph (p. 203); Results > Other responses, only paragraph (p. 209)
evidence.extracted: What was rated as hallucinatory behaviour at these amounts was, as the authors describe it, illusory experiences in all sensory domains, that is distortions of real stimuli; ideas of reference, paranoid content and loosening of associations are described at the larger amount. On that day 8 of the 18 people (4 men and 4 women) had blurred vision, about half of them with horizontal nystagmus, and 2 women vomited; at follow-up interview nobody reported lingering or recurrent effects such as nightmares, flashbacks or perceptual change, although that follow-up was unstructured.

evidence.locator: Results > Behavioral Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; > Positive Symptoms, 1st paragraph; > Negative Symptoms, only paragraph; Figures 1 to 3 and their legends (p. 111); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 114)
evidence.extracted: In 15 healthy men given four infusion conditions in randomized order, with ratings made blind to condition, psychosis-like scores rose with the condition (BPRS positive subscale F3,42 = 21.84, P < .0001), as did a clinician-rated negative-symptom scale (SANS total F3,42 = 10.55, P < .0001), while the BPRS negative subscale changed more weakly (F3,42 = 2.89, p = 0.047), a result that does not meet the adjusted threshold of 0.025 the authors apply on p. 114 and that their own list of robust findings replaces with the SANS total. Across baseline, infusion and washout the BPRS total showed a condition x time interaction of F6,83 = 17.62 (p = 0.0001), the positive subscale accounting for the largest part (F6,83 = 22.54) and the negative subscale for a smaller one (F6,83 = 2.73, p = 0.02). All the printed dose-to-dose p values are one-tailed.

Negative-symptom subscales during the steady-state conditions (placebo, low, moderate, high): affective flattening 0.2, 0.0, 0.7 and 1.4 (F3,42 = 4.49, p = 0.008); alogia 0.0, 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6 (F3,42 = 2.51, p = 0.07); avolition-apathy 0.2, 0.2, 0.5 and 1.5 (F3,42 = 9.08, p = 0.0001); anhedonia-asociality 0.3, 0.2, 0.8 and 2.9 (F3,42 = 6.51, p = 0.001); attention 0.9, 0.9, 0.5 and 1.3 (F3,42 = 2.61, p = 0.06), which is not ordered by the amount given. The standard deviations are as large as the means or larger. The authors state that the clinical syndrome produced was mild, that people stayed comfortable, alert and oriented, and that no abnormal symptoms were found at the assessment about 48 hours after the infusion, which was abbreviated and unblinded.

evidence.locator: Results > Plasma ketamine levels (3.1), only paragraph
evidence.extracted: In the open study, blood ketamine during the scans ran from 240 to 1145 ng/mL (mean 557, SD 254). Psychotic symptoms appeared on average 4.5 minutes after the start of the infusion, at a mean blood level of 386 ng/mL. Blood levels did not correlate significantly with the metabolic changes, but did correlate with the AMDP 'schizophrenic' syndrome score (P < 0.05), a score whose per-person values the paper does not print.

risk_of_bias.note: Blinding is unverifiable or broken in every study read in full (cards sc_krystal_1994, sc_malhotra_1996, sc_newcomer_1999, sc_vollenweider_1997a and sc_vollenweider_1997b, all rated high overall); the review selected each study's peak value by design, and 9 of its 36 studies were not double-blind, 3 of them unblinded. Against the downgrade: blinding status did not change the review's pooled effect significantly in any of the three outcomes, and the review's own across-study summary rates performance and detection bias low. The downgrade is kept, because that is a contrast between studies, no primary study checked whether blinding held, and the peak-value selection is untouched by it.

inconsistency.note: I2 75.7%, 74.9% and 64.6% in the review's Results (its abstract prints a range of 77% to 83%, which matches none of them); prediction intervals about 0.28 to 2.72, 0.44 to 2.65 and 0.39 to 1.93 (editors' calculation on the card, reproduced independently by the second reader); the direction is consistent.

imprecision.note: 725 people across 36 studies; the pooled intervals are narrow.

publication_bias.note: Egger z = 4.27, 5.06 and 5.12, all P < .001; trim-and-fill estimates 1.37, 1.49 and 1.09 remain large and are stated in the claim.

grade.reasoning: Within-person, placebo-controlled laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order start high (METHODS 6.3; round brief). Risk of bias -1: no study read in full reports a blinding check, the condition produced visible signs in nearly half the people at the larger amount in one study, the main outcomes are clinician ratings and self-ratings, one of the two imaging studies had no dummy condition at all, and the pooled estimates are peak values chosen at each study's largest amount and highest-scoring rating time (the review's confidence is rated low with AMSTAR 2, provisionally, because one item can be judged only from a supplement neither reader opened). The review's own finding that blinding status did not change the pooled effect in any outcome counts against that downgrade; it is kept because the comparison is between studies rather than within them, because no primary study checked whether blinding held, and because the peak-value selection is unaffected by it. Inconsistency -1: heterogeneity across the pooled studies is high (I2 65% to 76% in the Results), subgroup analyses did not explain most of it, and the editors' prediction intervals run from about 0.3 to 2.7, so the size of the effect is uncertain even though its direction is not. Not downgraded for indirectness, because the claim is restricted to healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein in a laboratory. Not downgraded for imprecision: 725 people and narrow intervals around each pooled estimate. Not downgraded for publication bias, although the Egger tests were significant for all three outcomes, because the trim-and-fill estimates stay large and the claim carries both; a reading that counted that asymmetry as a further downgrade would give very low. Rated as worded, including the size. A claim worded only to the direction and the short duration would sit a level higher, because every one of the 36 pooled studies found an increase and the laboratories read in full agree. Overlapping evidence (METHODS 6.3): Newcomer et al. (1999) is one of the 36 pooled studies, in the total and the positive analyses, so it is not independent of the pooled estimates; Malhotra et al. (1997), a separate report, is pooled as well (the review does not say whether it shares participants with Malhotra et al., 1996), while Krystal et al. (1994) is not among the 36; at least 8 of the 36 list a review author among their authors; and the two 1997 studies come from the same Zurich laboratory. How long the effects last is carried by the two studies that rated people again after the infusion stopped, and by nothing else: the review gives no recovery time, states that the time course has still to be characterised, and took its ratings during the session.
